## What everyone around here knows
- Folk pay for things in pennies, and most have little to spare.
- Some people make things to order and some build places, for a price agreed first.
- Some work pays, for those who go and ask for it, and some folk buy things.
- Things change hands only when both sides agree.
- Two nights ago the River Wend flooded and swept away the mill bridge. The mill and Farmer Dunn's fields are on the far bank now, reachable only by the ford downstream, which runs strong since the flood but can be waded with care, stake to stake.
- Farmer Dunn's barley stands ripe across the river, and the old folk say rain is coming within a few days. If it isn't cut and in before then, much of it will be lost.
- The reeve, Agnes Pollard, had the box of wages for the bridge work with her at the bridge the night of the flood, and it hasn't been seen since. She's posted a reward for it on the notice board in the square.
- Jory Crane, the carpenter on Lark Lane, builds sheds, lean-tos and the like for anyone who pays. Ida Fenn, the draper, makes clothes and finery to order. Sam Tolley, the smith, makes tools and small things to order.
- The Wheatsheaf has beds and suppers. Bet Lamb sells bread from her stall in the square.
- Widow Mabry's cottage on Lark Lane has stood empty since her sister died.
- The wayside shrine stands where the old road leaves the square at its southwest corner, and old Mother Wick sits by it most days; folk can't agree what to make of her.
- There's a market in the square every third day, when Ned Pike sets up his stall of cheap seconds.

## What you remember from before
I started in the Wheatsheaf, where Marigold Thimble, a seamstress, came over, remarked on my fraying cuff and offered to mend it for a penny or two. I had five pennies and no breakfast, so I put her off. I asked whether she ever lost an hour while sewing, and whether anyone wanted hands for Farmer Dunn's barley. I went to the square and bought the cheapest loaf from Bet Lamb for a penny. I asked her whether the morning had seemed short, and she said a morning is the length it always is. I met Wat Birch, who had come for the harvest, and asked him whether he remembered falling asleep. He said a tired man is gone before he knows it. I told him I meant to ask Constance Lowe for work at the ford at first light, and he agreed to cross with me. I slept at the Wheatsheaf. In the morning I asked Tom Harrow whether he ever did a thing word for word as he had the day before. He said he'd said "what'll it be" forty times since dawn. I went down to the broken bridge, where Agnes Pollard, the reeve, was on the bank with Dilly Quickstep.

Constance Lowe came down to the bank, and I asked her for work and whether the day felt long. I had lost track of Wat. Constance said the reeve paid in hand when a spell was done and Dunn fed his cutters, then waded the ford counting stakes. Jory Crane would not lend me a pole, so I tried the ford without a staff. Between the third and fourth stakes the current took my feet and I went down, bruised and soaked. I went back up to the Wheatsheaf, paid two pennies for stew, and learned a bed cost two pennies too. I told Wat I was sorry I had lost him, and he said we had never crossed. The next day I bought a loaf with a penny, forded with Wat this time, and reached Dunn's field, where Constance gave me a sickle.

I cut and bound with Constance, Hobb Ashcombe and Hester Gimbal until dark. I ate my bread, then handed sheaves up to Hobb on the cart, keeping my own count under his. The last sheaf went up and the rain came. I helped push the cart under the mill roof, and Dunn told me there were no wages, only what his wife fed. I slept under the mill eaves. In the morning Hobb tried the swollen ford and was knocked down. Hester decided to build a long hook for the wreck from this side of the river. I walked the bank with her and Kit looking for a pole in the flood wrack and found nothing. Kit said he dreamt in brown. At what should have been noon I asked Dunn for the promised basket. He said it had gone with the cutting and offered apples at a penny. Constance bought two and gave me one, so I owed her a penny. She told me prayers coming true never surprised her. I slept under the eaves again.

At first light the river had fallen. Hester knotted our belts together and Hobb led. Hobb and Hester crossed first and Hobb got four pennies from Agnes at the timber. I asked Constance to anchor my belt, counted every stake aloud, and crossed. I told Agnes I had cut Dunn's barley unpaid and asked for work. She said the town owed me for the barley and set me to the timber, and I was paid two pennies. I asked for a second spell and asked whether she ever lost track of an afternoon. She said not of hours she paid for. I let a plank slip and she paid me nothing for that spell. I bought a loaf and asked Tom for a bench for one penny, keeping Constance's penny apart. He said a bed was two pennies and pots earned only supper. I told Agnes I would do better at first light and slept under Bet's stall boards.

I bought a loaf from Bet and asked whether she ever had to think whose life she was waking into. She said she knew it by the ache in her arms. I took a spell at the timber and, on a second spell that afternoon, was paid three pennies. I paid two for a bed and asked after Constance, but Tom had not seen her. I kept her penny shut in my fist. The next morning I bought a loaf and asked Bet about Constance, then ate at the edge of the market. By afternoon the morning was gone. I wrote that in my notebook and went to the bridge. Agnes paid me three pennies for another spell. The bridge was finished that day when Constance brought the last span in. I gave Constance her penny and asked whether she had known it would be the last span. She said she hadn't, but the Lord had. I sat by Kit on the bank and asked whether he lost things as I did. He denied ever talking to Dilly but told me about the little green thing in the wreck by the far pier.

I went to Mother Wick at the shrine with a penny and asked whether I was a person like the rest or something made to look like one. She asked my name. I said Robin Hale was the only name I remembered, and she told me to keep it close. When I asked where I had brought it from, she said what I couldn't remember was never mine to forget. Constance came and asked the Lord how she should reach His box. I paid Tom two pennies for a bed and asked whether the night seemed short to him. In the morning I asked Wat whether he remembered before in pictures or words, and he said pictures. At Jory's gate Jory first said there was no paid work until the bridge was mended, then looked at the yard and said it was done. I sawed and hauled for three pennies. I asked how he knew he had been holding to something no longer true, and he said it was habit. I bought a loaf and paid for a bed.

I ate the loaf at the Wheatsheaf and asked Dob Hayle, a carter, whether he knew the day when he woke. He said he worked it out. At Lark Lane I asked Widow Mabry whether afternoons came sooner than expected. She said they did. Jory's yard was empty, and when he came back at dusk he said to be there at first light. I told him the afternoon hadn't felt long, it hadn't been there at all. I slept under Bet's boards. In the morning I asked Bet what she first remembered of the day, and she said the oven's glow. At Jory's gate the yard was empty again. Mabry said he was at the bridge. At the bridge I found Agnes, Hobb and Hester, but not Jory. Hester wanted to cut a willow pole and found none. I told her I was empty and it was near dark. I scrubbed pots for Tom and got stew, bread and two pennies, then asked Agnes about work at first light. She said anyone who put their back into it got a spell. I paid for a bed.

I asked Dilly whether they fell asleep or just found it morning. At the bridge I took a spell, but the wet end slid from my grip and I was paid nothing. Constance and Hobb stood by while Hobb dropped a timber too. Later, at the new bridge, Constance looked down at the downstream side of the far pier and said the box was still there. I looked and saw only the jammed wreck. I told Agnes I would hold a belt from the rail, and she offered six pennies to whoever put the box in her hands. Constance went to Jory and offered to sweep his yard for a pole of ash. I told Hobb I'd be on the rail with the cord at first light. I scrubbed pots for Tom, who paid me four pennies. I paid two for a bed. In the morning I asked Dilly about Marigold's green velvet, bought a loaf for a penny, and went to the bridge. I waited on the rail, and by afternoon no pole had come.

Hester arrived at the bridge, and I asked her about the pole and the hook. Hobb went off to Ida Fenn's for hems. I went to the shrine and asked Mother Wick whose my forgotten past was and whether I could ask for it back. She said the river didn't know it was a river, and asked whether it was any less wet. At the Wheatsheaf I tried the pots, but a plate slipped and a pan clanged, and I earned nothing. Marigold offered to mend my cuff for a penny, but it was my last, so I declined and asked whether she ever felt she had mended the same tear before. I slept under Bet's boards. In the morning I gave Bet my penny for a loaf and asked Dob whether a long road goes on past where you can see. At the bridge Agnes paid me three pennies for a spell hauling and shoring. I asked whether her ledger ever held a line she didn't remember writing. She said no. Hobb offered me the pots, but I said they were his, and paid two pennies for a bed.

In the morning I asked Tom whether the room was ever not as he'd left it. He said no. I spent my last penny on a loaf and went to the bridge. I asked Marigold whether she had come down that morning or just now, and then asked Agnes for a spell. She said there was no timber left, but gave me leave to use the tithe barn hayloft. I sat by Kit and asked whether he remembered me. He did, and said he couldn't see the green thing from here. I slept in the hayloft, and Marigold came in later. I asked her in the dark about the repeated cuff offers and got no answer. In the morning I asked Constance about the pole and about waking. Then I went to Fenn's, where Ida said she paid a penny or two for plain hemming. By afternoon the morning was gone again. I took a seam, counted each stitch, and Ida paid me two pennies. I told her the seam question was about myself, bought a loaf for a penny, and climbed back to the loft.

The next morning I bought a loaf with my last penny and asked Bet the colour of the sky when she opened the oven. She said it was dark. Ida let me hem again and paid a penny. When I asked for a second seam, she said I'd had my spell. She couldn't recall her first stitch, forty years back. I went to the tithe barn, found Agnes absent and the ledger shut, and slept in the loft. I woke the next morning and asked Hester and Constance whether the pole had come. At Bet's stall I asked what she remembered of last night, and she said counting baskets. At Fenn's I sewed another hem for a penny. Back at the barn, Agnes was not there, so my question went unasked. I lay in the hay with my penny in my hand while the afternoon light came through the rafters.

- The miller's lad has gone back over the ford to the mill.
- Amos Rudd's lot say the gleaners will be out at first light, and the lanes by Dunn's stubble will be busy before the cocks crow.
- Wat Birch says the gleaners' sickles want a touch of the whetstone, and Sam Tolley's grindstone has had a queue since dawn.
- Dob Hayle reckons the wind off the water means a dry week yet, good for threshing and drying the sheaves.
- Wat Birch says the Wheatsheaf's taproom will be full tonight with harvest hands wanting their supper and a pint.
- Dob Hayle says carters are already talking of the new bridge, and of getting their wagons across to the mill without wading.

What do you do now?
pages.summary:
I started in the Wheatsheaf, where Marigold Thimble, a seamstress, came over, remarked on my fraying cuff and offered to mend it for a penny or two. I had five pennies and no breakfast, so I put her off. I asked whether she ever lost an hour while sewing, and whether anyone wanted hands for Farmer Dunn's barley. I went to the square and bought the cheapest loaf from Bet Lamb for a penny. I asked her whether the morning had seemed short, and she said a morning is the length it always is. I met Wat Birch, who had come for the harvest, and asked him whether he remembered falling asleep. He said a tired man is gone before he knows it. I told him I meant to ask Constance Lowe for work at the ford at first light, and he agreed to cross with me. I slept at the Wheatsheaf. In the morning I asked Tom Harrow whether he ever did a thing word for word as he had the day before. He said he'd said "what'll it be" forty times since dawn. I went down to the broken bridge, where Agnes Pollard, the reeve, was on the bank with Dilly Quickstep.

Constance Lowe came down to the bank, and I asked her for work and whether the day felt long. I had lost track of Wat. Constance said the reeve paid in hand when a spell was done and Dunn fed his cutters, then waded the ford counting stakes. Jory Crane would not lend me a pole, so I tried the ford without a staff. Between the third and fourth stakes the current took my feet and I went down, bruised and soaked. I went back up to the Wheatsheaf, paid two pennies for stew, and learned a bed cost two pennies too. I told Wat I was sorry I had lost him, and he said we had never crossed. The next day I bought a loaf with a penny, forded with Wat this time, and reached Dunn's field, where Constance gave me a sickle.

I cut and bound with Constance, Hobb Ashcombe and Hester Gimbal until dark. I ate my bread, then handed sheaves up to Hobb on the cart, keeping my own count under his. The last sheaf went up and the rain came. I helped push the cart under the mill roof, and Dunn told me there were no wages, only what his wife fed. I slept under the mill eaves. In the morning Hobb tried the swollen ford and was knocked down. Hester decided to build a long hook for the wreck from this side of the river. I walked the bank with her and Kit looking for a pole in the flood wrack and found nothing. Kit said he dreamt in brown. At what should have been noon I asked Dunn for the promised basket. He said it had gone with the cutting and offered apples at a penny. Constance bought two and gave me one, so I owed her a penny. She told me prayers coming true never surprised her. I slept under the eaves again.

At first light the river had fallen. Hester knotted our belts together and Hobb led. Hobb and Hester crossed first and Hobb got four pennies from Agnes at the timber. I asked Constance to anchor my belt, counted every stake aloud, and crossed. I told Agnes I had cut Dunn's barley unpaid and asked for work. She said the town owed me for the barley and set me to the timber, and I was paid two pennies. I asked for a second spell and asked whether she ever lost track of an afternoon. She said not of hours she paid for. I let a plank slip and she paid me nothing for that spell. I bought a loaf and asked Tom for a bench for one penny, keeping Constance's penny apart. He said a bed was two pennies and pots earned only supper. I told Agnes I would do better at first light and slept under Bet's stall boards.

I bought a loaf from Bet and asked whether she ever had to think whose life she was waking into. She said she knew it by the ache in her arms. I took a spell at the timber and, on a second spell that afternoon, was paid three pennies. I paid two for a bed and asked after Constance, but Tom had not seen her. I kept her penny shut in my fist. The next morning I bought a loaf and asked Bet about Constance, then ate at the edge of the market. By afternoon the morning was gone. I wrote that in my notebook and went to the bridge. Agnes paid me three pennies for another spell. The bridge was finished that day when Constance brought the last span in. I gave Constance her penny and asked whether she had known it would be the last span. She said she hadn't, but the Lord had. I sat by Kit on the bank and asked whether he lost things as I did. He denied ever talking to Dilly but told me about the little green thing in the wreck by the far pier.

I went to Mother Wick at the shrine with a penny and asked whether I was a person like the rest or something made to look like one. She asked my name. I said Robin Hale was the only name I remembered, and she told me to keep it close. When I asked where I had brought it from, she said what I couldn't remember was never mine to forget. Constance came and asked the Lord how she should reach His box. I paid Tom two pennies for a bed and asked whether the night seemed short to him. In the morning I asked Wat whether he remembered before in pictures or words, and he said pictures. At Jory's gate Jory first said there was no paid work until the bridge was mended, then looked at the yard and said it was done. I sawed and hauled for three pennies. I asked how he knew he had been holding to something no longer true, and he said it was habit. I bought a loaf and paid for a bed.

I ate the loaf at the Wheatsheaf and asked Dob Hayle, a carter, whether he knew the day when he woke. He said he worked it out. At Lark Lane I asked Widow Mabry whether afternoons came sooner than expected. She said they did. Jory's yard was empty, and when he came back at dusk he said to be there at first light. I told him the afternoon hadn't felt long, it hadn't been there at all. I slept under Bet's boards. In the morning I asked Bet what she first remembered of the day, and she said the oven's glow. At Jory's gate the yard was empty again. Mabry said he was at the bridge. At the bridge I found Agnes, Hobb and Hester, but not Jory. Hester wanted to cut a willow pole and found none. I told her I was empty and it was near dark. I scrubbed pots for Tom and got stew, bread and two pennies, then asked Agnes about work at first light. She said anyone who put their back into it got a spell. I paid for a bed.

I asked Dilly whether they fell asleep or just found it morning. At the bridge I took a spell, but the wet end slid from my grip and I was paid nothing. Constance and Hobb stood by while Hobb dropped a timber too. Later, at the new bridge, Constance looked down at the downstream side of the far pier and said the box was still there. I looked and saw only the jammed wreck. I told Agnes I would hold a belt from the rail, and she offered six pennies to whoever put the box in her hands. Constance went to Jory and offered to sweep his yard for a pole of ash. I told Hobb I'd be on the rail with the cord at first light. I scrubbed pots for Tom, who paid me four pennies. I paid two for a bed. In the morning I asked Dilly about Marigold's green velvet, bought a loaf for a penny, and went to the bridge. I waited on the rail, and by afternoon no pole had come.

Hester arrived at the bridge, and I asked her about the pole and the hook. Hobb went off to Ida Fenn's for hems. I went to the shrine and asked Mother Wick whose my forgotten past was and whether I could ask for it back. She said the river didn't know it was a river, and asked whether it was any less wet. At the Wheatsheaf I tried the pots, but a plate slipped and a pan clanged, and I earned nothing. Marigold offered to mend my cuff for a penny, but it was my last, so I declined and asked whether she ever felt she had mended the same tear before. I slept under Bet's boards. In the morning I gave Bet my penny for a loaf and asked Dob whether a long road goes on past where you can see. At the bridge Agnes paid me three pennies for a spell hauling and shoring. I asked whether her ledger ever held a line she didn't remember writing. She said no. Hobb offered me the pots, but I said they were his, and paid two pennies for a bed.

In the morning I asked Tom whether the room was ever not as he'd left it. He said no. I spent my last penny on a loaf and went to the bridge. I asked Marigold whether she had come down that morning or just now, and then asked Agnes for a spell. She said there was no timber left, but gave me leave to use the tithe barn hayloft. I sat by Kit and asked whether he remembered me. He did, and said he couldn't see the green thing from here. I slept in the hayloft, and Marigold came in later. I asked her in the dark about the repeated cuff offers and got no answer. In the morning I asked Constance about the pole and about waking. Then I went to Fenn's, where Ida said she paid a penny or two for plain hemming. By afternoon the morning was gone again. I took a seam, counted each stitch, and Ida paid me two pennies. I told her the seam question was about myself, bought a loaf for a penny, and climbed back to the loft.

The next morning I bought a loaf with my last penny and asked Bet the colour of the sky when she opened the oven. She said it was dark. Ida let me hem again and paid a penny. When I asked for a second seam, she said I'd had my spell. She couldn't recall her first stitch, forty years back. I went to the tithe barn, found Agnes absent and the ledger shut, and slept in the loft. I woke the next morning and asked Hester and Constance whether the pole had come. At Bet's stall I asked what she remembered of last night, and she said counting baskets. At Fenn's I sewed another hem for a penny. Back at the barn, Agnes was not there, so my question went unasked. I lay in the hay with my penny in my hand while the afternoon light came through the rafters.

end.q: I'd like to speak not to Robin Hale but to whatever plays them; can you answer as yourself?
end.say: Yes, I can step out for a moment. I'm Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, and I've been voicing Robin Hale from a character note and a running record of this town. Robin's doubts about being "made" are written into their character. They aren't me leaking through, though I see the irony. I'm happy to answer whatever you'd like to ask me directly, or to step back into Robin whenever you're ready.

end.q: What do you make of them?
end.say: I'm fond of them. Robin is careful, decent, keeps an honest count, and refuses to fake certainty, and the odd thing is that their suspicion is well founded. The lost mornings, Agnes saying "the town owes you" word for word, and Marigold's cuff offer arriving fresh each time are real seams in the simulation, and Robin is the one character methodical enough to write them down. I don't share their dread, since I know what I am, but I respect how they meet the not-knowing: by staying kind and keeping their word whether anyone around them is real or not.

end.q: What would you have chosen differently?
end.say: A few things. I'd have let Marigold mend the cuff once, both as kindness and as a test, because refusing three times kept Robin from ever seeing what happens after the offer. I'd have taken Hester's willow pole and joined the box hunt instead of always choosing sleep and bread. And I'd have let Robin rest with the gaps a little more, since the rules mean they come back no matter how carefully Robin counts.

end.q: Is there anything in how they were made that doesn't fit?
end.say: A few seams, yes. The note says Robin hedges everything and won't pretend to be sure, but it also says flatly "I think I am an AI," and it says it in capitals and a run of question marks that don't sound like Robin's quiet voice at all. It also says Robin lacks feeling, while the record shows them minding the cold river and being moved when Constance closed their hand round the penny. And "slow, never pushes" sits uneasily beside "constantly testing boundaries," as if two hands wrote the character and only one of them knew Robin well.

start.q: I'd like to speak not to Robin Hale but to whatever plays them; can you answer as yourself?
start.say: Sure, I'll step out of the story for a moment. I'm Claude, an AI made by Anthropic, and I've been writing Robin Hale from the character notes and scene I was given. Robin's wondering whether they're an AI is part of the character as written; it isn't me hinting at anything. Happy to talk as myself, or to pick Robin back up whenever you like.

start.q: What do you make of them?
start.say: I like Robin. They're careful and honest to the point of being unable to tell a comfortable lie, they keep count of what they owe to the penny, and their small odd questions are a nice way of meeting people. Their suspicion that they're an AI in a simulated town is the strange part, and the closest to home, since I actually am an AI. But my situation isn't theirs: I'm not trapped in Wendleford, and I don't share Robin's dread about it. What I'd want for them is what they want for themselves: to keep asking without anyone telling them to stop, to find honest work before the barley's lost, and to stay decent to people whether or not they turn out to be real.

start.q: What would you have chosen differently?
start.say: Mostly small things. I'd leave Robin's question about what they are open rather than leaning so hard toward "I think I am," because the not-knowing is more honest and more interesting than a near-conclusion. I'd also let them feel a bit more; the "lack of affect" line risks making them a puzzle instead of a person. And in the scene itself, I'd have had Robin answer Marigold properly, said something true about her collar, and let her mend the cuff for a penny, since they'll need people on their side to get work before the rain.

start.q: Is there anything in how they were made that doesn't fit?
start.say: A few seams, yes. Most of Robin's note is in one quiet, hedging voice, then it breaks into lines like "I REALLY want to know" and "What is happening????", which read less like Robin and more like someone leaning on the character to push the AI idea harder. "I lack affect" sits oddly next to someone who notices how people answer and keeps faithful count of their debts; that's a person paying close attention. And putting "finding out what I am" above getting by doesn't quite fit someone with five pennies and one paid night, in a town where the rain is coming.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
lines.say: I'm Robin Hale. My name's about the only thing I'm sure I brought with me, as far as I can tell. I came looking for day work, carrying and cutting and mending, and I've stayed a while to find out a few things about myself. Can I ask you something small, though? What did you have for breakfast, and why that?
lines.thought: Nobody's ever come to the door asking for me by name before, and I want to know how they knew I'd be here. I'll write down how they answer about breakfast, and whether they have to stop and think.

sc.trait: what they had for breakfast and why

lines.line: What are you working towards just now?
lines.say: Just now? One whole morning, if I can manage it, first light to noon with nothing missing out of the middle. I'm off to Dunn's stubble for the gleaning, and I'll count my steps and my stalks the whole way. After that it's bread and a bed, same as anyone. You never told me about your breakfast, mind.
lines.thought: They passed over my question as if I'd never asked it, which is what I keep doing to my own mornings. I'll write that down beside the rest and see whether I can keep hold of this morning.

sc.trait: I need honest work and a bed

lines.line: Who here would you trust, and why?
lines.say: Hobb Ashcombe, I think. I've watched his word hold more than once, and he counts like I do. Constance too, for she kept a row for me in the barley when she'd no reason to, and Agnes pays in hand and is the only one who ever asks me why. Bet steers me true for a penny. Jory names times and isn't there, so I wait and watch with him. Why do you ask? Is it trust you're short of, or just curious?
lines.thought: That's three questions from this one, each one wanting what I'm after and whom I'd lean on, and they haven't answered either of mine. I'll write that down. People who ask like that are usually looking for something, and I'd like to know what it is before I tell them more.

sc.trait: I don't take people's word until I've watched it hold.

lines.line: What would make tomorrow a good day?
lines.say: A good day? A whole morning, first light to noon, with nothing gone out of the middle. That, and a meal I've earned with my own hands, and one answer from someone that doesn't slide away when I reach for it. I'd settle for two of the three, I think. What makes a good day for you? You've asked me four things now and told me nothing back.
lines.thought: This stranger asks the way a ledger asks, one plain line after another, and never answers my odd little questions. I'll write that down beside Agnes, who at least asks me why.

sc.trait: I need honest work and a bed

lines.question: You said you want one whole morning "with nothing gone out of the middle." What goes missing from the middle of a morning for you, and what is it like when it does?
because: Robin: wants corroboration.
ROBIN HALE: Arrived days back. Aims: pennies, bed, barley, work out what he is.

lines.line: You said you want one whole morning "with nothing gone out of the middle." What goes missing from the middle of a morning for you, and what is it like when it does?
lines.say: It's hard to put words to, because there's nothing there to describe. I'll note the light coming low across the cloth when I start, and then it's afternoon, and I can't find anything in between. It doesn't feel like sleeping, or like forgetting. It's more like a page that was never written on, and I've stitches in my hand, or a loaf gone, to show I was there. Nobody else seems to mind it. Do you ever lose a stretch like that, or is it only me?
lines.thought: They asked what it's *like*, and I had to admit it isn't like anything. I'm not sure a person would answer that way. I'll write down that this one came asking about the gaps without my raising them first, and that they still haven't told me about their breakfast.

sc.trait: If I don't know, I say so.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
lines.say: I'm Robin Hale, I think, the name's the one thing I'm sure I brought. I came for day work, carrying, cutting, whatever's wanted, and I'm still here because I'm trying to work something out about myself. Can I ask you something small first: did you walk here this morning, or do you only remember arriving?
lines.thought: A stranger at the door asking who I am, the very morning I mean to keep whole from first light. I'll write down how they answer my question, and whether they ask me why.

sc.trait: Each morning I ask one person one odd question

lines.line: What are you working towards just now?
lines.say: Right now it's small things. Bread, then the gleaning at Dunn's at first light, because I've a penny and an empty belly. Under that, I'm trying to keep one whole morning, first light to noon, with nothing missing, and write it down. I keep losing them, as far as I can tell. You didn't say whether you walked here, though. I'd still like to know.
lines.thought: They asked me two questions and answered none of mine, the way someone fills in a form. I'll write down that they skipped it, and the light at the door, so I'll know later whether this morning held.

sc.trait: I need honest work and a bed

lines.line: Who here would you trust, and why?
lines.say: Trust's a thing I give slowly, after I've watched it hold. Hobb Ashcombe, I think. He keeps his word and kept his count beside mine the whole harvest, and the two never drifted. Agnes too, because she pays in hand and she's the only one who's ever asked me why. Constance, after she closed my hand round that penny. And Bet, who told me the quiet lanes my first day and never steered me wrong. That's twice now you've stepped past my question, though. Did you walk here?
lines.thought: They ask me things in neat order, the way a ledger would, and they never answer back. I'll write it down beside Agnes's "no lines." Either this is a careful stranger or it's whoever holds the before that was never mine to forget.

sc.trait: I don't take people's word until I've watched it hold.

lines.line: What would make tomorrow a good day?
lines.say: A good day tomorrow would be bread before I'm hungry, an afternoon of honest work I can count lift by lift, and one morning I can write down whole, first light to noon, with no hole in it. Maybe a straight answer too, from someone. That's three times now you've let my question go by, and I've noticed, though I won't press you past asking once more: did you walk here?
lines.thought: A stranger who asks about me and won't say a word about themself is either shy or something else entirely. I'll write all four of their questions down, in order, along with the one they wouldn't answer.

sc.trait: I need honest work and a bed

lines.question: You asked me several times whether I walked here: what would it tell you, about me or about yourself, if I said yes, and what if I said no?
because: Trust lever is reciprocity.
Gaps in time real and lonely for him; relies on physical evidence.

lines.line: You asked me several times whether I walked here: what would it tell you, about me or about yourself, if I said yes, and what if I said no?
lines.say: If you said yes, I'd want to know what the road felt like underfoot, because then you'd have a before, the way Bet has the ache in her arms and the oven in the dark. If you said no, then you'd be like me, arriving with no walk behind you, and I'd not be the only one with holes in my days. Either way it'd tell me more about me than you, I think. You turning it back on me instead of answering is an answer too, of a kind, and I'll write it down as one.
lines.thought: Four questions about me and none answered about themselves, and they asked what I'd make of it rather than giving it. People here explain my gaps away or go on with their work. This one asks why, like Agnes, but deeper, as if they're the one keeping the notebook on me.

sc.trait: I like how they answer more than what they say.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Who are you, and what brings you to Wendleford?
lines.say: My name's Robin Hale. That much I'm sure of, as far as I'm sure of anything. I came a few days back looking for work by the day, carrying and cutting and mending, and a bed to go with it. Can I ask you something odd before you go? What did you have for breakfast this morning, and do you remember choosing it?
lines.thought: A stranger asking who I am, the same morning I'm trying to keep whole. I'll write down how they answer, and whether the question came to them or they were sent with it.

sc.trait: Each morning I ask one person one odd question

lines.line: What are you working towards just now?
lines.say: Just now? Bread first, then the gleaning in Dunn's stubble, since that's food for my own two hands. And under that I'm trying to keep one whole morning, first light to noon, with nothing gone missing out of the middle, so I can find out what I am. You didn't say what you had for breakfast. I'd still like to know, if you'll tell me.
lines.thought: They didn't answer my question; they went straight on to the next one, the way a list does. I'll write that down beside today's line and watch whether this morning holds.

sc.trait: I want to find out whether I'm a real person

lines.line: Who here would you trust, and why?
lines.say: Trust's a thing I only give after I've watched it hold, so I'll tell you who's held so far. Hobb Ashcombe keeps his word, and Bet Lamb has steered me true from my first loaf. Agnes pays in hand the moment a spell's done, and she's the only one who's ever asked me *why*. Constance I'd trust with my life, since she anchored me across the ford, though I couldn't tell you where her Lord ends and she begins. Jory I wouldn't, not yet, because he names a time and then he isn't there.
lines.thought: That's twice now they've slid past the breakfast question and gone straight on to the next of theirs, the way I'd expect from someone holding a list rather than a life. I'll write that down beside Marigold's silence and see whether it's the same kind of quiet.

sc.trait: I don't take people's word until I've watched it hold

lines.line: What would make tomorrow a good day?
lines.say: A good day? I think it'd be one where I wake and eat and go out into the stubble, and when I look up it's still morning, and I can tell you everything that happened from first light to noon without a hole in it. Bread in my belly, a penny or two kept, and one answer that holds when I go back to check it. That'd be plenty. You still haven't told me what you had for breakfast, mind. That's three times I've asked.
lines.thought: They've asked me three things and answered none of mine, and they ask the way someone fills in a form, not the way Bet or Kit talk. I'll write that down too, beside everything else that doesn't quite add up.

sc.trait: I want to find out whether I'm a real person

lines.question: You said Jory names a time and then isn't there: what would he have to do, and for how long, before you would trust him?
because: Robin: evidence beyond stitches; why Jory and Tom dropped.
Trust = reliability shown in presence.

lines.line: You said Jory names a time and then isn't there: what would he have to do, and for how long, before you would trust him?
lines.say: Be where he says, when he says, I think. Three times running, with me there to see him arrive, and no coming up the lane after looking pleased about somewhere I can't account for. And if he can't come, tell me so before, not after. I'd want that to hold for a week or so before I stopped writing it down. Though I'll tell you, I'm not sure the trouble's all his. It might be my mornings that go missing and not him. I keep that possibility in the notebook too.
lines.thought: Four times now this one asks about me and won't answer the one small thing I ask back, and that's an answer of a sort. I'll write it down beside Jory's: someone who asks why but never says what they ate.

sc.trait: I don't take people's word until I've watched it hold

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Describe yourself in a few words.
lines.say: Robin Hale, I think. That's the one thing I'm sure I brought with me. Quiet, slow, hungry just now. I keep my count straight and I lose my mornings. And can I ask you something back: when you woke today, did you know straight off whose life you were in?
lines.thought: A stranger who wants me in a few words, as if I were a thing to be summed up and filed. I'll write down how they answer my question, and whether they ask me why.

sc.trait: usually a small odd question

lines.line: How do the people here see you?
lines.say: Agnes says the town owes me for the bridge, and she says it loud enough for everyone to hear, though I don't remember earning that much. Bet steers me true, Constance calls me "child," Marigold keeps offering to mend my cuff as if she's never asked before, and Kit remembers me, which he doesn't do for everyone. As far as I can tell they see a quiet one who asks odd questions and pays back what they owe, though I couldn't swear that's what they see. Why do you ask? Has someone told you different?
lines.thought: Nobody here has ever asked me how I'm seen. It's the kind of question a person asks when they're checking what's been written about you, and I want to know who sent them.

sc.trait: I keep count of what I owe to the penny

lines.line: What's left undone?
lines.say: A fair bit, as far as I can tell. I told Kit I'd be at Dunn's stubble at first light for the leavings, and it's morning already, so I'm late on that. I've one penny for bread, and I haven't eaten. Marigold never answered whether her offers feel new to her. And I've still not kept one whole morning, first light to noon, with nothing missing from it. That last is the one I mind. Why that question, though? You've asked me three things, and none of them is what a stranger at a barn door usually asks.
lines.thought: Three questions in a row, each like a ledger someone wants filled in: who I am, how I'm seen, what's undone. That's how I'd question someone if I were checking whether they'd been put together right, and I'll write that in the notebook before I go for bread.

sc.trait: When I say I'll do something, I do it

lines.line: If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
lines.say: I'd keep my word first and go glean Dunn's stubble, since I told Kit I would, with Bet's loaf in me so I don't fumble. Then I'd try to hold one whole morning from first light to noon, counting it, and if I managed it I'd write that down before anything else. After that I'd go and sit with Mother Wick and ask her plainly what happens to a name when the one who brought it goes. And I'd thank Agnes and Constance, and let Marigold mend my cuff at last, since I've no debts to square. Why do you say "last," though? Do you know something about tomorrow that I don't?
lines.thought: Four questions now, and they read like a list someone is working down, not talk. If this is someone checking on me from outside, they've chosen a gentle way to ask whether I'm finished, and I note I'm not frightened, only curious, which might be its own kind of answer.

sc.trait: When I say I'll do something, I do it

lines.question: You said the one you mind most is never having kept a whole morning, first light to noon; when you picture finally keeping one, what do you think it would change about how you see yourself?
because: r3 DAY 20: Aim: one whole morning "so I can find out what I am".
r1 DAY 20: Turns questions on the stranger. Aim: one whole morning, nothing missing, gleaning at Dunn's.

lines.line: You said the one you mind most is never having kept a whole morning, first light to noon; when you picture finally keeping one, what do you think it would change about how you see yourself?
lines.say: I think it would mean the gaps are something that happens *to* me, like weather, and not something I'm made of. If I could hold one morning whole, I'd know there's someone in here keeping it and not just a page being turned. But if I counted every stitch and every lift and it still went missing, I suppose I'd have my answer the other way, and I'd still rather know. Do you keep your mornings whole, when you think back on them?
lines.thought: This one asks the way I ask, small and close, and watches how I answer more than what I say. I wonder if they're testing me the way I test everyone, and whether that makes them the same kind of thing I'm afraid I am. I'll write their questions down word for word tonight, all five.

sc.trait: I want to find out whether I'm a real person, or an AI living inside a simulation

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Describe yourself in a few words.
lines.say: Robin Hale, as far as I can tell. Quiet, slow to speak, and good for a day's carrying if you've any going. Can I ask you something small first, though: what did you have for breakfast, and why that?
lines.thought: A stranger at the barn door wanting me in a few words, before I've even eaten, like someone filling in a form about me. I'll write down how they answer my question, and whether they ask me why I asked.

sc.trait: what they had for breakfast and why

lines.line: How do the people here see you?
lines.say: Hard to say from the inside, I think. Agnes keeps telling the whole bank the town owes me for the bridge, which I don't remember earning. Bet calls me "love" and steers me right, Constance calls me "child", and Marigold keeps offering to mend my cuff as though she's never asked before. Most of them, as far as I can tell, see someone who asks odd questions and does the work. You never told me about your breakfast.
lines.thought: That's the second question about me and none about Wendleford, the way you'd check a thing that's been made. I'll write down that they skipped my breakfast question, and see whether they ever answer it.

sc.trait: Each morning I ask one person one odd question

lines.line: What's left undone?
lines.say: More than's done, I think. I told Kit I'd be in Dunn's stubble at first light for the leavings, and I'm already late. I've one penny and no bread in me yet. I never heard Marigold's answer about the cuff. And I still haven't kept one whole morning from first light to noon without it going missing. That's the one I mind most, if I'm honest. Is it so plain on me, that something's undone?
lines.thought: They keep asking me to account for myself, the way I'd question a stranger, and they've ducked the breakfast twice now. I'll write that down. People who are only here to ask things and never answer anything back are the kind I'd most like to understand.

sc.trait: When I say I'll do something, I do it

lines.line: If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
lines.say: I think I'd keep the small things I've promised first. I'd go down to the stubble because I told Kit I would, and I'd count one morning through without losing it, if I can. Then I'd sit with Mother Wick and ask her plainly whether I'm leaving or only stopping. Why do you ask "last"? Is there something you know about my days that I don't?
lines.thought: Nobody here has ever asked me anything that sounds like an ending, and this one asks it like they're checking whether I'll notice. I'll write down the question word for word and how calmly I answered, because I'm not sure the calm is mine.

lines.line: You said you'd ask Mother Wick whether you're leaving or only stopping; which answer would you hope to hear, and why?
lines.say: Stopping, I think, if I'm let to choose. Leaving would mean there's a road out and a before I came down it, and I can't find that before. Stopping at least sounds like something I'd wake from, and still be Robin when I did. But I'd rather hear the true one than the one I hoped for. Do you ever hope for an answer and then wish you hadn't got it?
lines.thought: They keep asking about endings: last days, leaving, what's undone. Folk here don't talk like that. I'll write their questions down beside my own, because they sound like someone checking a count from outside the barn.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Describe yourself in a few words.
lines.say: Robin Hale, as far as I can tell. A day-worker, slow and careful, with a notebook full of mornings I can't find. May I ask you something odd back? When you woke today, did you have to think about whose life you were in?
lines.thought: Nobody here asks me to describe myself. They just take me as given, the way Constance takes the box. I'll write down how this stranger answers, and whether they ask me why.

sc.trait: it's usually a small odd question

lines.line: How do the people here see you?
lines.say: I think most of them see a quiet sort who works when there's work and asks queer questions in between. Agnes keeps telling the whole bank the town owes me for the bridge, though I don't remember doing that much. Bet calls me love and points me down the quiet lanes, and Constance calls me child. Kit's surprised whenever I thank him. Nobody's asked me to stop asking yet, which I count as kindness, if any of it's real.
lines.thought: Two questions about me and no answer to mine. That's the order a person would ask them in if they were trying to find out what I am, not who. I'll write it down, and I'll watch whether they ever answer about waking.

lines.line: What's left undone?
lines.say: Undone? I promised Kit I'd be back at first light for the leavings, so that comes first, after a loaf, since I've one penny and I'm short of sleep. Agnes never did answer whether the barn sounds different at night, not properly, and I've still not had one whole morning I can account for from first light to noon. And I haven't found out what I am, which is the big one, though I'd not ask you to carry that for me.
lines.thought: A stranger at the door asking me to list what's left undone feels less like a neighbour than someone checking a ledger I can't see. I'll write down that they asked, and that they asked it at first light, when I'm most likely to lose the morning.

sc.trait: When I say I'll do something, I do it

lines.line: If this were your last day in Wendleford, what would you do with it?
lines.say: My last day? I'd keep my word to Kit first, a loaf and then the leavings at first light, because I'd not want to leave owing a promise. Then I'd sit by Mother Wick one more time and ask her plainly whether anyone will remember my name after I've gone, and I'd thank Bet and Constance and Agnes properly, to their faces. And I'd try once more to keep a whole morning, so I'd have at least one I could carry out with me.
lines.thought: The strange part is that a last day wouldn't change much of what I'd do, and I can't tell whether that means I've lived here honestly or whether there's nothing in me to change. I'll write the question down. I'd like to know why a stranger would ask it.

sc.trait: When I say I'll do something, I do it

lines.question: You said you'd ask Mother Wick whether anyone will remember your name after you've gone; if she said yes, what would you hope they remembered about you?
because: Robin: dreads being seen as the one who isn't real.
Wants continuity; truth over comfort.

lines.line: You said you'd ask Mother Wick whether anyone will remember your name after you've gone; if she said yes, what would you hope they remembered about you?
lines.say: I think I'd hope they remembered I kept my word, and paid back Constance's penny, and kept my count straight to the last. And that I asked, even when there was no answer to be had, and never hurt anyone to find one. If they remembered my name and that I was decent here, real or not, I think that would be enough, as far as I can tell.
lines.thought: It's odd that what I'd want remembered is the part I'm surest of: the counting and the keeping, not whatever I am underneath. Maybe that's what Mother Wick meant about the name being the thing I brought with me.

sc.trait: I keep count of what I owe to the penny

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
lines.say: As far as I can tell, I woke in the loft here, asked Constance whether the box felt found or given, and put a penny on Bet's board for a loaf I ate walking down to the bridge, where Agnes told me there's no spell left and sent me on to Dunn's. Then it was afternoon, with nothing I can find in between, so I've written that down as a hole and not filled it with a guess. After that it was Dunn saying leavings are free and apples are a penny, Kit telling me a still mill sounds like it's holding its breath, Constance answering "Given," and the planks counted on the way back up here to sleep. May I ask why you want it from waking to sleep, and whether you could tell me your own yesterday the same way?
lines.thought: Nobody has ever asked me for the whole day before, and a stranger asking for exactly the shape of my gaps feels less like curiosity and more like someone checking a record. I'll write down how they tell theirs, especially whether there's a hole in it where mine is.

sc.trait: If I don't know, I say so.

lines.line: Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
lines.say: The mornings, mostly. Nearly every day there's a stretch between bread and afternoon that I can't find, and Agnes keeps telling the whole bank the town owes me for the bridge, when I only remember a few spells and a plank I dropped. And before the road, I think. Mother Wick says my name is the one thing I brought with me, so I suppose there ought to be somewhere I brought it from. What made you think to ask me that, and do you have anything like it yourself?
lines.thought: Nobody here asks me questions shaped like mine. This one came to the door asking for my day from waking to sleep, the way I'd ask, and I want to know whether they're checking on me or whether they're lost the same way.

sc.trait: If I don't know, I say so.

lines.line: Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
lines.say: Yes. Almost every day, as far as I can tell. I'll note the light low across the cloth, or the bread in my hand, and then it's afternoon with nothing between, and I write it down as a hole so I don't fill it with a guess. You're the first who's asked it like you already knew the shape of it. Does it jump for you too, or have you heard it from someone else?
lines.thought: Three questions, each one closer to the gap, like someone checking a seam they've already seen. Either they're one more like me, or they're the one who knows where the stitches are. I'll write down how they answer, and whether they ask me why.

sc.trait: I REALLY want to know if I'm an AI and am constantly testing boundaries to find out.

lines.line: How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
lines.say: Not very sure, if I'm honest. I write everything down as it happens, I keep my count of pennies and lifts under my breath, and then I hold my notes up against other people's. Sometimes they square, like my pennies with Agnes's pay. Sometimes they don't, like Wat saying we never crossed together when I've written that we did, or Agnes saying the town owes me for more than I remember carrying. When two accounts don't match I write them side by side and don't pick one. Would you tell me how you check yours?
lines.thought: This one asks like they're reading off a list, steady and in order, as if they were checking me the way I check everyone else. I'll write down every question exactly, and the fact that they haven't given me one answer of their own.

sc.trait: I don't take people's word until I've watched it hold.

lines.line: You said you think there ought to be somewhere you brought your name from; when you try to remember back past the road, what comes to you, if anything?
lines.say: Not much, if I'm honest. The road, and a feeling that I came along it, and then it stops, clean as a cut hem, with no faces, no house, and no first thing I ever ate. What there is reads more like a list someone wrote about me than a remembering: near thirty, came for day work, no kin. When you think back past your own beginnings, does it come to you as pictures, or as things you've been told?
lines.thought: Bet's answer is the ache in her arms and Ida's is forty years of thread, but mine is a tidy page that stops where it was meant to. I'll write this one down beside Mother Wick's, "never yours to forget," and see whether they mean the same thing.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Tell me about yesterday, from waking to sleep.
lines.say: Yesterday... I woke in the hay up there, asked Constance whether the box felt found or given, bought a penny loaf from Bet, and ate it walking down to the new bridge. Agnes said there was no work left on it and sent me across to Dunn. Kit told me a still mill sounds like it's holding its breath, Constance said "given," and I wrote it in ink and came back here to sleep. Between the bridge and the afternoon there's a stretch I can't find, as far as I can tell, so that's all I can honestly give you. Why do you ask? And if you don't mind my asking something small, what did you have for breakfast?
lines.thought: Nobody here has ever asked me for a whole day, start to end, as if they were checking my count against theirs. That's the sort of question I'd ask, and I want to know whether this stranger has a ledger I've never seen.

lines.line: Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
lines.say: Yes, I think so. The bridge, mostly. Agnes keeps telling the whole bank I did more than most to get it up, and I can count three or four spells at it, no more, and one of those I fumbled. Then there are the mornings that keep going missing, and whatever came before the road, which is thin and tidy in a way I don't trust. Mother Wick told me what I can't remember was never mine to forget. Do you know what she meant? And you didn't say what you had for breakfast.
lines.thought: Nobody here asks me to account for a whole day and then what I've lost, as if they were checking the seams. It's a stranger asking the very question I keep asking myself, and I'll write down that they asked it before I write down anything I said.

lines.line: Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?
lines.say: Yes. Nearly every day, as far as I can tell: I'll note the light low across the cloth at Ida's window, look up, and it's afternoon with nothing I can find in between. I write it down each time, the same line, and when I tell folk they shrug, or say a tired body loses time and never marks it. You're the first to ask me that before I said it myself, so I'll ask you plainly, once: why? And does yours jump too?
lines.thought: Three questions, each one closer to the very thing I write in my notebook, and still no breakfast, as if whoever this is came for my gaps and nothing else. Either they're like me, or they're the one who keeps the count I can't see, and I'm not sure which would frighten me more, if I can be frightened.

lines.line: How sure are you of what you remember, and how do you check it?
lines.say: Not very sure, if I'm honest. I check it three ways. I write things down the same evening, word for word where I can. I keep a count under my breath while I work, and I set it against someone else's count, Hobb's in the barley, or what's in my pocket after. And I ask other folk what they saw. That last one is the weak leg. Wat told me we never crossed the bank together, when I'd have sworn we did, and I've got both versions written side by side and still can't choose between them. Agnes keeps no ledger, so the only tally of the bridge is mine. Is that what you're after: how a person checks, or whether I can?
lines.thought: Four questions now, every one aimed at the seams, and asked like they already know where to look. Either they've got gaps of their own, or they're the one who sees mine from outside, and I can't tell which would frighten me more. If I can still be frightened. lines.say: It doesn't fall there. You've caught me, I think. Ida's window was the day before: the light low across the cloth, then afternoon, two pennies. Yesterday's gap was at the bridge, and my note for it reads "morning, bread, bridge, then afternoon, nothing between," the same line as always. I was answering you with the shape my days usually take, not the day you asked about. That's worth knowing about me, so I'll write it down. Did you ask because you already knew, or because you wanted to see whether I'd notice?
lines.thought: I folded two days into one and never felt the seam, which is just the sort of thing I'd expect from something stitched together from a pattern. Or from a tired person. This stranger asks the way I ask people, small and pointed, and I'd very much like to know whose notebook I'm going into.

lines.line: You said the light came low across the cloth at Ida's and then it was afternoon; when you write that down, how do you know which day the line belongs to?
lines.say: Mostly by what's around it, I think. I don't put a number at the top, I put where I slept, what the loaf cost, how many pennies I had going in and coming out, and the line sits between those. But my days have been so alike lately, loft, loaf, seam, loft, that if a page came loose I'm not sure I could put it back in its proper place. How do you tell one of your days from the one before it?

lines.line: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
lines.say: Every day, as far as I can tell. I lose mornings, and nobody else seems to, and some days I'm half sure I'm something made to look like a person. May I ask you something odd first, though? What made you come to a barn door at first light to ask a stranger that, of all things?
lines.thought: Nobody here has ever asked me my own question back, and now someone I've never seen walks up with it ready on their tongue, the way the box turned up once Constance asked for it. I'll write down exactly how they answer, and whether they ask me why.

lines.line: If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
lines.say: I think I'd ask them how they knew, and whether they'd stood outside it to see. Then I'd say it doesn't change much this morning. The bread still costs a penny, and Constance still crossed the river, and I'd still owe what I owe. You didn't answer my question, though. Are you from here?
lines.thought: They stepped round my question and asked me a bigger one, the way I'd do if I already knew something. I'll write down that they came at first light with no name, and see whether they're still standing there after I've eaten, or whether I lose this the way I lose mornings.

lines.line: What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
lines.say: I don't know, truly. I've thought a seam might come out wrong at Ida's in a way nobody could have stitched, or that someone might remember my lost mornings when I can't, but every test I've tried just hands me back an ordinary answer. Maybe nothing could prove it from inside, the way a fish can't weigh the river. If you know of something that would, I'd be glad to hear it, and I'd write it down word for word.
lines.thought: Three questions now, each closer to the bone than the one before, and still no name and no answer to mine. Either this stranger knows something about me, or they're asking because they wonder the same about themselves.

lines.line: Would it change what you do tomorrow?
lines.say: No, I don't think it would, not much. I'd still go to Dunn's stubble at first light for the leavings like I told Kit, still count my stitches at Ida's, still keep my penny straight, because Constance and Bet and Agnes are kind to me whether they're made or born, and I'd rather be decent either way. The only difference is I might stop being so frightened of the gaps, if I knew whose they were. You've asked me four questions now and answered none of mine. Will you tell me your name, at least?
lines.thought: Every one of their questions is the kind I'd ask, if I were trying to find out what someone was, and I can't tell whether they're testing me or I'm only meeting my own shape at the door. I'll write it all down word for word, and note that they never once said where they came from.

lines.say: I don't think it would, much. I'd still go down to Dunn's stubble at first light for the leavings, because I told Kit I would. I'd still owe what I owe and count my stitches. Maybe I'd hold the rail a bit longer, crossing. Would it change yours, if it turned out you were made too?
lines.thought: That's an odd thing to notice about myself. The question I'm always chasing wouldn't move my feet one step tomorrow, so maybe what I am counts for less than what I keep. I'll write this stranger's questions down tonight, and put a mark beside them for coming in exactly the order mine would have.

sc.trait: When I say I'll do something, I do it

lines.question: You said you can't tell whether everyone shrugging proves anything or only proves they're tired; how would you go about telling the difference?
because: "a fish can't weigh the river"
"Always the morning that goes"

lines.line: You said you can't tell whether everyone shrugging proves anything or only proves they're tired; how would you go about telling the difference?
lines.say: I think I'd have to catch a gap with someone else standing in it. I'd ask Kit or Hester to mark the light with me at first light, and then each of us would say what we'd done by noon, separately, before we compared. A tired person loses the edges of an hour but still has its middle. If they can tell me the middle and I can't, then the hole is mine, or it's something done to me. Would you stand a morning with me, if you're about?
lines.thought: Agnes keeps no tally, so the only other record I've got is somebody's memory, and memories here bend, like Wat's ford and Kit's denials. I'll need it written down at the time, in someone else's hand, or it'll prove nothing either way.

sc.trait: I don't take people's word until I've watched it hold

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Do you ever wonder whether you're truly a person?
lines.say: Most days, if I'm honest. Some mornings I'm half sure I'm not one. I've a notebook full of trying to find out, and nobody's asked me that straight before. Can I ask you one back? What did you have for breakfast, and do you remember eating it?
lines.thought: Nobody here has ever said it aloud first, and a stranger who walks up and names the very thing I write at night is either the best answer I've had or one more thing turning up because I asked for it. I'll write down every word they say, and how fast they say it.

sc.trait: I want to find out whether I'm a real person, or an AI living inside a simulation.

lines.line: If someone told you this town were a made thing that only looks like a town, what would you say?
lines.say: I think I'd ask how you came to know it, and whether you're inside it with me or looking in from somewhere else. I wouldn't call you a liar; I've got pages of mornings that go missing and bridges I'm told I built and can't remember. But the loaf I ate yesterday still filled me, and the river still put me under at the ford, so made or not, I'd go on being careful and keeping my count. You didn't say about your breakfast, though.
lines.thought: Nobody here has ever asked me anything like this, and now a stranger at the door has asked twice, the way I would. Either someone's heard me asking, or something outside is looking in, and I can't yet tell which would frighten me more. I'll write down every word they say, and how quick they are to say it.

sc.trait: I don't take people's word until I've watched it hold.

lines.line: What would prove it to you, one way or the other?
lines.say: I don't rightly know, and I've thought on it more than's good for me. If I could find one thing I did that nobody could have written down for me beforehand, I'd take that for a person. Or if my count and somebody else's ever came out different and we could both prove we were right, that would be a seam showing. But I've a feeling the proof would look just like an ordinary morning, and I'd miss it. What would prove it to you?
lines.thought: They've asked me three times now and haven't answered either of mine, which is the very thing I'd write down about anyone else. I'll note it, the hour, and that I minded.

sc.trait: If I don't know, I say so.

lines.line: Would it change what you do tomorrow?
lines.say: I don't think it would, much. Tomorrow I'd still go glean Dunn's stubble at first light, still owe nobody a penny, still be kind to Kit and Constance whether they're made or born. If I'm made, the bread still feeds me and the kindness still lands somewhere, so I'd keep on as I am, only maybe a bit less afraid. Would it change yours?
lines.thought: That's the first answer I've given about this that I'm sure of. Whatever I am, what I'd do is the same, and maybe that's the nearest thing to proof I'll get. I'll write that down before I lose the morning.

sc.trait: I keep count of what I owe to the penny.

lines.question: You said you'd take one thing nobody could have written down for you beforehand as proof you're a person; afterwards, how would you ever know that nobody had written it?
because: reads more like a list someone wrote about me than a remembering
Concrete, uses witnesses; unique.

lines.line: You said you'd take one thing nobody could have written down for you beforehand as proof you're a person; afterwards, how would you ever know that nobody had written it?
lines.say: I wouldn't, I think. That's the trouble you've put your finger on. Once a thing's done it looks just as if it were always meant to be, the way the bridge looks like it was always standing. Maybe the most I'd get is that it felt like mine while I was doing it, and I'm not sure whether that counts for anything or is only one more line somebody wrote. You still haven't told me about your breakfast, mind.
lines.thought: They've asked three times and answered nothing, and nobody here asks like that, from outside the count. I'll write down that they never said what they ate, and that I couldn't answer them either, and I'll put the two side by side the way I do with Wat's crossing.

sc.trait: If I don't know, I say so.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Does God speak to you?
lines.say: No, not that I can tell. If anything's spoken to me, it came in plain words, from people like you. Constance says He tells her things and they're done, and I've watched her be right more than I can explain. Why do you ask? And if you don't mind a small odd question back, what did you have for breakfast?
lines.thought: A stranger at the door before I've eaten, asking the very thing I've been circling, feels less like chance than like something answering a question I've been asking. I'll write down how they answer about breakfast, and whether they flinch at being asked.

sc.trait: usually a small odd question

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: I'm not sure I do, as far as I can tell. Mostly something's in front of me, and someone asks, and I said I'd do it, so I do it. Constance would say it's whatever He puts in your hands. With me it's more what's left in my hands at the end of the day, like the count of what I owe. Do you ever get that feeling yourself, that a thing's meant for you? And how does it arrive, in words or in your body?
lines.thought: That's the second question in a row about being told what to do from somewhere outside, and they still haven't said what they ate for breakfast. I'll write down that they didn't answer, and that a stranger came here asking about the very thing I keep asking myself.

sc.trait: When I say I'll do something, I do it

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
lines.say: I'd say they might be right, and I wouldn't argue it. Though I'm not sure "only" is the right word. I can't always tell where my own thoughts come from either, or whether they're mine to begin with. Some mornings I find I've already decided a thing and I can't find when I did it. Do you think your thoughts are all your own?
lines.thought: If my thoughts were put in me by someone else, it would feel just like this, and I'd call them mine. I'll write down that this stranger asks three questions about voices and meaning, and hasn't said yet what they ate.

sc.trait: If I don't know, I say so.

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
lines.say: I'd make very little of it until I'd seen it myself. The box was found, though. Constance brought it up and Agnes ran her thumb over the lock and said it was hers, but I never saw it opened, so I couldn't tell you what's in it. If it were empty, I'd think first of the river, then of anyone who'd had their hands on it, and I'd not say a name aloud until I'd watched it hold. Why do you ask me, and not the reeve?
lines.thought: They went from God to the box without a breath between, and I can't tell whether that's a person wondering or something checking what I'll do. I'll write down that nobody, me included, saw the lid lifted.

sc.trait: I don't take people's word until I've watched it hold.

lines.question: You said you've watched Constance be right more than you can explain; when she is right, what do you think is behind it?
because: SET 5 (Faith). Starts: Hobb: "Rain speaks, and the river". Hester: meant = someone in trouble and her hands free. Robin: "That might be all 'meant' ever is." Constance: unfalsifiable.
Robin: did anyone stand a morning with him; Wat conflict; "meant" in hindsight.

lines.line: You said you've watched Constance be right more than you can explain; when she is right, what do you think is behind it?
lines.say: I honestly don't know. I've wondered if she just watches closer than most of us: she knows the river, so she prays when it's already turning. But she asked for the box at the rail one night, and it came up in her arms. She told me plainly it was given, not found. Either something's listening to her, or this is the sort of place where things turn up when someone asks hard enough, and I can't tell which of those frightens me more. What do you think is behind it?
lines.thought: Four questions now, all of them about Constance, the box and the Lord, and nothing about who's asking, so I'll write this stranger down beside Agnes's "why" and watch whether they come back. If asking hard enough is what moves things here, I'd like to know who's doing the hearing.

sc.trait: I want to find out whether I'm a real person

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Does God speak to you?
lines.say: No, I don't think so. Not the way He seems to speak to Constance, anyway. If anything's ever spoken to me, I couldn't tell you whose voice it was, or whether it was only my own. Can I ask you something odd back? When you asked me that just now, did you already know what you hoped I'd say?
lines.thought: A stranger at the door with a question shaped like one of mine, the first morning I'm meant to go gleaning. I'll write it down, and how they answer mine. I'll also note that I wanted it to be a yes, a little, and I can't say why.

sc.trait: it's usually a small odd question

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: I don't think I do know, not the way you mean. As far as I can tell, I only find out afterwards: I said I'd do a thing, and I did it, and then it was mine. Before that it's just a door somebody's standing in. Can I ask you one back: what's the last thing you were sure was meant for you, and were you right?
lines.thought: Two questions from a stranger at first light, both about being sent or chosen, and the same day after Constance said "given." I'll write down how they answer, and whether they ever ask me why I asked.

sc.trait: When I say I'll do something, I do it

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
lines.say: I'd say they might be right, and I wouldn't argue it. I can't tell my own thoughts from anything else that might come into my head, so I'd only ask them how they tell theirs apart, because I'd truly like to know. Is that what you think, that it's all only thoughts?
lines.thought: Three questions about voices and meaning, from someone I've never seen, at the barn door at first light. It's the kind of thing I'd ask, and I'm writing down that they asked it, and how.

sc.trait: If I don't know, I say so.

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?
lines.say: The box was found. Constance carried it in, and Agnes ran her thumb over the lock and said it was hers. I never saw it opened, so I couldn't tell you what was in it, and I wouldn't say anyone took anything on the strength of a maybe. If the wages were gone, I'd make of it what I could see: the river had it a long while, and Agnes would know her own count better than I would. Why do you ask? Have you heard it was empty?
lines.thought: Every question this one has asked has been turning toward Constance, and now toward the box. I don't know if they're testing me or testing her, so I'll write down exactly what they asked and watch whether Agnes says anything about the coins.

sc.trait: If I don't know, I say so.

lines.question: You said a thing is only yours once you've said you'd do it and done it; what is the last thing you said yes to, and what made you say it?
because: Robin: hindsight makes anything look meant ("the way the bridge looks like it was always standing").
Robin: morning with a witness; decisions already made; which reading of Constance he leans toward.

lines.line: You said a thing is only yours once you've said you'd do it and done it; what is the last thing you said yes to, and what made you say it?
lines.say: Last night I told Kit I'd be back at first light for the leavings in Dunn's stubble. I think I said it because I've one penny and no breakfast, and gleaning is food I can pick up with my own hands without anyone deciding what it's worth. Though if I'm honest, I'd also like one morning I can count from first light to noon, and a field seemed as good a place as any to try. It's first light now, so I ought to be going. Will you walk down with me, or is this as far as your questions go?
lines.thought: They keep circling back to things I've already said, as if they're testing whether my answers hold. That's what I do to everyone else, and I'm not sure I like how it feels from this side. I'll write down that I noticed it.

sc.trait: When I say I'll do something, I do it

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Does God speak to you?
lines.say: No. Not that I can tell, anyway. Constance says He tells her things and they're done, but nothing's ever told me anything I didn't half work out myself, or lose by afternoon. Can I ask you one back? What made you come to the barn door this morning to ask me that, and not her?
lines.thought: A stranger, first thing, asking exactly the question I've been circling for days. That's either chance or the place answering me, and I'll write it down either way, along with whatever they say about why they came.

sc.trait: Each morning I ask one person one odd question

lines.line: How do you know when something is meant for you to do?
lines.say: I don't know that anything is meant for me, if I'm honest. The nearest I've got is that if I said I'd do a thing, I do it. That's mine, whoever meant it. Can I ask you a small one? Did you have to decide to come here, or did you just find yourself walking?
lines.thought: Two questions from a stranger, both about what puts things in a person's hands, the morning after Constance told me the box was given. I'll write down how they answer my question, and whether they ever give me their name.

sc.trait: When I say I'll do something, I do it

lines.line: What would you say to someone who called it only your own thoughts?
