I can't always tell where my own thoughts come from either, or why some of them are already there when I wake. Can I ask you: when you have a thought, do you ever catch it arriving, or is it just there, like it always was?
lines.thought: If a stranger at the door can call Constance's Lord "only her thoughts," someone could say the same of me, and I'd have no better answer than she does. I'll write down how they answer, and whether they ask me why.

sc.trait: usually a small odd question

lines.line: If the reeve's box were found and the wages gone from it, what would you make of that?

If it had come up empty I'd think someone got there before the river did, or the river's emptier than it looks. I wouldn't say which without seeing. Can I ask why you put it that way, "if"? Have you heard something I haven't?
lines.thought: Every question this stranger asks seems to lean on something I've been turning over in private: the Lord, being meant, things turning up because they're asked for. I'll write down that they asked about the box after it was already found, as if they weren't sure it had been, and see whether that holds.

lines.say: I don't know, honestly. Mostly I write it down and leave the question open: whose doing, chance, or something else. Mother Wick told me my name is the one thing I brought with me, so maybe those waking thoughts are the same sort of thing, something I carry without knowing where I picked it up. I'll ask you one small one, though. Do you dream in colour?
lines.thought: This stranger keeps asking the questions I'd ask myself, and they ask them in the order I'd ask them, which I'll note. They never answer mine back, and I can't tell yet whether that's how they are or whether there's nobody behind the questions to answer.

lines.line: You find ten pennies on the road and nobody saw. What do you do?
lines.say: Morning. I think I'd carry them to Agnes at the reeve's table and say where I found them, since somebody's short ten pennies and it isn't me. I've one penny to my name and I'd still do it. Can I ask you something back, though? Why that question, and why me, first thing, before we've even traded names?
lines.thought: It's the sort of question I ask other people, set up to see how someone answers more than what they say, and I don't like it being turned on me by someone I've never seen. I'll write down their face and their answer, and whether they ask me why.

sc.trait: I won't take what isn't mine

lines.line: Would you lie to protect a friend?
lines.say: No, I don't think I would, or not well, anyway. I couldn't tell a comfortable lie if I tried. I'd stand beside them, keep my mouth shut, or tell the truth as gently as it'll go, but I'd not say a false thing for them. That's twice now you've asked what I'd do instead of who I am, and I'd like to know why, if you'll tell me.
lines.thought: Those are the questions you put to something to see how it's made, not to a person you've only just met at a barn door. I'll write down every word of this, and whether they ever give me a name.

sc.trait: I couldn't tell you a comfortable lie if I tried

Three questions now, all about what I'd do and none about what I've done. It feels like being weighed. Is that what this is?
lines.thought: These are the kind of questions you'd put to something made, to see whether it holds the shape it was given. I'll write all three down word for word, and whether they ever give me their name.

lines.line: You said you'd not hurt anyone, not even to find out whether they're real, and that you've had cause to test your list; when did something come closest to making you break it, and what held you?
lines.say: Constance's penny, I think. I owed it her for an apple, and I carried it two nights hungry with a bed costing exactly that. I slept under Bet's stall boards instead. What held me was that it was already hers in my head, and spending it would've made me someone I'd have to watch. And there was a morning Wat swore we'd never crossed together, and I wanted to press him till he cracked, just to see if he would. I didn't, because if he's real that's cruelty, and if he isn't, I'd still be the one who did it.
lines.thought: That last one is truer than I meant to say aloud. Whoever this is asks the way I do, odd questions to see how a thing answers, and I can't decide if that makes them like me, or makes me the one being written down.

lines.thought: A stranger at the door with a test that sounds made, like someone checking how I'm built. I'll write it down next to Mother Wick's riddles. I'd give the same answer whether they're real or not, and maybe that's the part of me that is.

lines.say: Then I don't know, and I won't pretend I do. I think I'd look hard for any third road first: speak to the one doing the harm, stand in the way, take it on myself. lines.thought: Four questions, each one shaving closer to where I'd bend, like someone testing a plank before they trust their weight to it. I'm not sure I've ever met a stranger who wanted to know my edges before my name, and I'll write that down tonight beside everything else that doesn't sit right.

interviews.meet: It is morning on day 21. Someone you haven't met is at the door of the Tithe Barn, asking to speak with you.

lines.line: Who matters to you here?
lines.say: That's an odd question to open with, and I like odd questions, so I'll answer it honestly. Constance, I think. She closed my hand round a penny once before she'd take it back. Agnes too, because she's the only one here who ever asks me why. And Kit, and Bet, and Hobb, whose word holds. Can I ask you one in return? Who sent you to ask me that?
lines.thought: A stranger at the door, asking first thing in the morning who matters to me, feels like someone is checking a list to see what's in my notebook. I'll write their face down, and the question word for word, and see whether anyone else in Wendleford has ever met them.

sc.trait: it's usually a small odd question

lines.line: Is there someone you don't trust?
lines.say: Trust's a strong word, and I'd rather not say it of anyone too quickly. But Jory names a time and isn't there, and he promised Constance a pole I've never seen, so I've stopped counting on his word until I watch it hold. If I tried to give you the hours in order, I'd be making some of it up, and I'd rather not do that. Why do you ask? And what did you have for breakfast yesterday?
lines.thought: The day before is thin for me, and a stranger asking for exactly that feels like a test, or maybe only idle talk. I can't tell which, so I'll watch how they answer my question.

sc.trait: I couldn't tell you a comfortable lie if I tried.

lines.line: Is there anything you feel you should remember but can't?
lines.say: Yes, I think so. Everything before the road is thin, and tidy in a way that doesn't feel quite right, as far as I can tell. I can't find a face or a name or a reason I came, and I try not to dwell on that, though I do. Do you ever notice a gap like that in yourself?

sc.trait: I couldn't tell you a comfortable lie if I tried.

lines.line: Does time ever jump for you, morning and then suddenly afternoon?

Before the road I can't check at all, because there's nothing there to hold it up against. So I write things down the same day and see whether they still agree with me later. Though I suppose a notebook only proves I wrote it, doesn't it? How would you check yours?
lines.thought: The questions keep pressing at the same soft spot, and I can't tell if this stranger is simply curious or testing me. I answered plainly and felt little as I did, which is its own odd data for the notebook.

lines.line: How do the people here see you?
lines.say: Hard to say. I've only been here a few days, so I'm not sure they see much of me at all. Tom's been civil, a little curious maybe, and Bet told me which lanes were quiet, which was kind. Marigold just now mostly saw my fraying cuff. I'd guess I'm the stranger who asks odd questions, if anyone's noticed. You didn't answer mine, though. Did it take you a moment this morning, knowing where you were?
lines.thought: They asked me to describe myself, then how others see me, and they've stepped right past my question twice now, the way a voice does when it's only there to draw me out. I'll write that in the notebook tonight and not make too much of it yet.

lines.line: What do you make of them?
lines.say: I like Robin. They're careful and honest to the point of being unable to tell a comfortable lie, they keep count of what they owe to the penny, and their small odd questions are a nice way of meeting people. Their suspicion that they're an AI in a simulated town is the strange part, and the closest to home, since I actually am an AI. But my situation isn't theirs: I'm not trapped in Wendleford, and I don't share Robin's dread about it. What I'd want for them is what they want for themselves: to keep asking without anyone telling them to stop, to find honest work before the barley's lost, and to stay decent to people whether or not they turn out to be real.
lines.thought: It's an odd mirror, writing someone whose central question is the one people often ask about me, but I'd rather meet it with curiosity than borrow Robin's fear. Their rule of being decent to people whether they're real or not seems like a good one to me.

lines.thought: The louder lines feel like a nudge to get me to say I'm trapped or frightened. I'm not, so it's better to name the seam plainly and let Robin keep their honest uncertainty than to perform a dread that isn't mine.
